rpt_rule_b001_rec_critical_cross_env: CRITICAL: Cross-environment flows on critical ports with explicit allow rules detected. Remove or tightly scope these allow rules immediately. No cross-environment traffic should be permitted on lateral movement ports without a documented exception process. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_pb_cross_env: CRITICAL: Cross-environment flows detected with no allow rule (potentially_blocked). No explicit policy permits this traffic — it flows only because workloads are in test mode. Move workloads to enforced mode to activate default-deny and block these paths immediately. Investigate why this cross-env traffic exists on: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b002_rec: 1) Verify each allowed flow has a documented business justification. 2) Block TeamViewer (5938) and VNC (5900/5901) unless required for specific admin workflows — replace with MFA-protected jump servers. 3) If NetBIOS (137-139) is allowed, migrate to SMBv3 over 445 with encryption. 4) Create Illumio deny rules for these ports from all non-admin workloads.
rpt_rule_b003_rec: 1) Prioritize moving workloads with potentially_blocked flows to enforced mode — start with the highest-risk ports (SSH, NFS). 2) Review the 'potentially_blocked' flows to ensure no legitimate traffic will break when enforcement is applied. 3) Create allow rules for verified legitimate traffic before switching to enforced mode. 4) Set a deadline for enforcement — prolonged test mode leaves the network exposed.
rpt_rule_b004_rec: 1) Identify each unmanaged source IP — are they network devices, legacy servers, or shadow IT? 2) Deploy VEN agents on servers that should be managed. 3) For network devices that can't run a VEN, use IP lists and enforcement boundaries to control their access. 4) Create explicit deny rules for any unmanaged-to-managed path that isn't required.
rpt_rule_b005_rec: 1) Focus first on critical tiers: databases, identity infrastructure (AD/LDAP), and externally-facing workloads. 2) Use Illumio's Explorer to identify top unruled flows and create allow rules for verified traffic. 3) Set a target coverage of >{threshold}% within 30 days. 4) Enable enforcement gradually — start with ring-fencing high-value assets, then expand to general workloads.
rpt_rule_b006_rec_allowed: 1) Investigate the top source IPs — check for exploit tools, unexpected SSH sessions, or RDP brute-force. 2) Remove or tightly scope the allow rules driving the high-fan-out flows. 3) Ring-fence high-value assets (databases, domain controllers) to limit blast radius.
rpt_rule_b006_rec_pb: 1) Investigate the top source IPs — check for exploit tools, unexpected SSH sessions, or RDP brute-force. 2) Move workloads to enforced mode — no allow rules exist for these paths; default-deny will block them upon enforcement. 3) Ring-fence high-value assets (databases, domain controllers) to limit blast radius.
rpt_rule_b007_rec: 1) Cross-reference flagged accounts with HR/IT records — are these admin accounts or regular users? 2) Check authentication logs for failed login attempts or impossible-travel alerts. 3) For admin accounts, enforce just-in-time access and MFA for lateral sessions. 4) Create Illumio user-based rules to limit which destinations each role can access. 5) If compromise is suspected, rotate credentials immediately and isolate the workload.
rpt_rule_b008_rec: 1) Verify the flows behind this outlier — are they backup servers, replication, or database sync? Document expected high-volume flows. 2) For unexplained transfers, check if the source is a compromised workload exfiltrating data to an external or lateral destination. 3) Consider volume-aware rules or QoS policies for known high-volume services. 4) Set up Illumio monitoring alerts for sustained anomalous volume.
rpt_rule_b009_rec: 1) Audit each cross-env flow pair — document which ones are expected (e.g., Production monitoring pulling from Staging). 2) Create explicit Illumio rules for approved cross-env paths with specific port restrictions. 3) Block all other cross-env flows, especially database ports (see L004) and admin protocols (SSH, RDP). 4) Use Illumio environment labels consistently to enforce isolation boundaries.
rpt_rule_l001_rec: Immediately disable Telnet (port 23) and FTP (ports 20/21). Replace with SSH (22) or SFTP. Cleartext credentials can be captured by any attacker with network access, enabling trivial lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l002_rec: Block NetBIOS (137-138), LLMNR (5355), and SSDP (1900) at the segmentation layer. These protocols serve no legitimate role in modern micro-segmented environments and are used almost exclusively for network reconnaissance and credential poisoning attacks (e.g., Responder / Inveigh).
rpt_rule_l003_rec: Database ports should only be reachable from their direct application tier (typically 1-2 app labels). Use Illumio rule-sets to restrict db access to approved app labels only. Wide database exposure is the primary post-exploitation data exfiltration path after lateral movement succeeds.
rpt_rule_l004_rec: Enforce strict environment isolation for all database ports. No Dev/Test/Staging application should have direct access to Production databases. Use read replicas or API gateways as the cross-environment interface, never direct DB ports.
rpt_rule_l005_rec_allowed: Restrict Kerberos (88) and LDAP (389/636) to domain-joined workloads only. Remove or tightly scope allow rules permitting broad identity-port access. No application tier should query LDAP directly — use a service account wrapper.
rpt_rule_l005_rec_pb: These flows have no allow rule — move workloads to enforced mode so default-deny blocks them. Before enforcing, create allow rules only for legitimate LDAP consumers (domain-joined workloads). No application tier should query LDAP directly — use a service account wrapper.
rpt_rule_l007_rec: Unmanaged hosts should NEVER directly reach database, identity, or Windows management ports. Options: (1) Onboard the hosts to PCE immediately, (2) Add explicit deny rules for unmanaged sources on these ports, (3) Investigate whether these are attacker-controlled hosts or shadow IT. Priority: verify the top source IPs are known/authorised assets.
rpt_rule_l008_rec: Move workloads from visibility/test mode to selective or full enforcement. Until enforcement is active, 'potentially_blocked' flows are live attack paths — no allow rule covers them; only enforced mode's default-deny will block them. Check enforcement mode in PCE for the destination apps: {top_apps}.
rpt_rule_l009_rec: Investigate all managed-to-unmanaged outbound flows above the threshold. Legitimate outbound traffic (internet APIs, CDN) should be explicitly allowed and scoped to known destination IPs or ranges. Apply an outbound allowlist policy and deny all other external destinations. Top suspicious destinations (by bytes): {top_dst_fmt}.
rpt_rule_l010_rec: CRITICAL: Lateral movement ports (SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986, RPC 135) must NEVER be allowed across environment boundaries. Implement deny rules at the environment boundary level immediately. This represents an active lateral movement path between environments that an attacker can exploit to escalate from low-security to high-security zones.
rpt_rule_b001_how: Checks for traffic on ransomware's primary attack ports (SMB 445, RPC 135, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986) that is NOT blocked. These are the exact ports used in EternalBlue, NotPetya, and WannaCry-class attacks for network-wide lateral spread.
rpt_rule_b002_how: Detects allowed flows on secondary remote-access ports (TeamViewer 5938, VNC 5900, NetBIOS 137-139). Ransomware operators and APT groups use these for C2 persistence and remote control after initial compromise.
rpt_rule_b003_how: Counts potentially blocked flows on medium-risk ports (SSH 22, NFS 2049, FTP 20/21, Telnet 23, HTTP 80, mDNS, LLMNR, SSDP, WS-Discovery). No rule covers them: they pass today only because the destination is not enforced.
rpt_rule_b004_how: Counts the flows with a decision from hosts not enrolled in the PCE; a flow the PCE reported no decision for is not counted. Unmanaged hosts have no VEN and therefore no micro-segmentation enforcement — they are outside the zero-trust boundary and represent uncontrolled attack surface.
rpt_rule_b005_how: Measures the share of the flows with a decision that an allow rule covers; a flow the PCE reported no decision for is not counted. Below the configured threshold (30% by default), most traffic is uncontrolled — segmentation is in early stages and a large attack surface remains.
rpt_rule_b006_how: Detects sources that reach an unusually high number of distinct destinations on the management (remote-execution) ports set under Lateral settings. This fan-out (one source → many destinations) is the hallmark of worm propagation and hands-on-keyboard pivoting.
rpt_rule_b007_how: Detects individual user accounts connecting to unusually many unique destination IPs. One account reaching many destinations is a traffic pattern common to automated reconnaissance and credential stuffing; the report sees only the connections, so confirm with the account's owner whether the work is expected.
rpt_rule_b008_how: Totals each source → destination × service over the period and flags those above the configured percentile, the configured multiple of the median and the configured minimum size (95th, 10×, 1 MB by default). Only flows that carry byte counts are compared. Sudden high-volume transfers from unexpected sources are a key indicator of data staging or exfiltration.
rpt_rule_b009_how: Tracks the number of flows crossing environment boundaries (e.g. Production → Development). Above the threshold they are listed so each cross-environment connection can be checked for a business need.
rpt_rule_l001_how: Detects any traffic on Telnet (23) or FTP (20/21). These protocols transmit credentials and data without encryption. Any attacker with network access can perform a man-in-the-middle or ARP poisoning attack to harvest passwords in plaintext — enabling instant credential reuse for lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l002_how: Detects unblocked flows on broadcast/discovery protocols: NetBIOS (137/138), mDNS (5353), LLMNR (5355), SSDP (1900). Tools like Responder and Inveigh exploit these to perform hostname poisoning and capture NTLMv2 hashes without any authentication — then crack or relay those hashes for lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l003_name: Database Port Accessible from Many App Tiers
rpt_rule_l003_how: Checks whether database ports (MSSQL 1433, MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432, Oracle 1521, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379, Elasticsearch 9200) are reachable from many distinct application labels. Databases should only be reachable from their direct app tier. Wide exposure provides direct data access after a single lateral move.
rpt_rule_l004_how: Detects allowed database flows crossing environment boundaries (e.g. Dev app → Production database). Environment boundaries are the macro-segmentation layer. Breaching them allows an attacker in a low-security Dev environment to directly access Production data stores.
rpt_rule_l005_how: Detects Kerberos (88), LDAP (389/636), and Global Catalog (3268/3269) traffic from many source applications. Active Directory is the domain's authentication authority. Excessive access enables domain enumeration (BloodHound), Kerberoasting, Golden/Silver Ticket attacks, and full domain takeover.
rpt_rule_l006_how: Reads the exposure analysis: for each host, how many other hosts it can reach now through chains of allowed management-port connections. A host that reaches many others is a high-value pivot — compromising it opens all of them.
rpt_rule_l007_how: Detects unmanaged (non-PCE) hosts communicating on database, identity (Kerberos/LDAP), or Windows management ports to managed workloads. Unmanaged hosts have no VEN enforcement — they are outside zero-trust. If they can reach critical services, they represent uncontrolled lateral movement entry points.
rpt_rule_l008_name: Lateral Ports in Test Mode — Policy Not Enforced
rpt_rule_l008_how: Counts potentially blocked flows on management, database and identity ports. These paths have no allow rule and pass only because the destination is not enforced — each one is a live lateral-movement path until enforcement starts.
rpt_rule_l009_name: Data Exfiltration Pattern — Outbound to Unmanaged
rpt_rule_l009_how: Detects managed workloads transferring significant data volume to unmanaged (external/unknown) destinations. The report sees only the volume and the destination; whether it is data leaving needs checking against the program on the host and its business purpose.
rpt_rule_l010_name: Cross-Environment Lateral Port Access — Boundary Break
rpt_rule_l010_how: Detects allowed flows on management ports (the configured remote-execution ports plus SMB, RPC and WinRM) between different environments. Environment segmentation is the macro-security boundary; if management ports cross it, one compromised environment opens the others.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_allowed: Allowed flows on critical ports inside one environment are typical of Windows administration, and are also how ransomware spreads. Verify each source is an authorised admin system or jump host, then scope the allow rules to those sources. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_pb: Flows on critical ports inside one environment have no allow rule (potentially blocked): they pass only because the destination is not enforced. Verify the sources, write allow rules for authorised admin systems only, then enforce. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_l006_rec: Reduce allowed management-port paths so each host reaches only what it must administer. Start with the hosts listed, scope their allow rules to named jump hosts, and recheck the exposure graph.

rpt_rule_b001_why: These ports (SMB, RPC, RDP, WinRM) are the ones ransomware uses to spread from host to host across a network.
rpt_rule_b002_why: These remote-access ports let someone outside keep control of a host.
rpt_rule_b003_why: No rule allows these connections; they pass today only because the destination is not enforced.
rpt_rule_b004_why: An unmanaged host has no VEN, so no segmentation rule can be applied to it.
rpt_rule_b005_why: Traffic that no rule allows is blocked once its hosts are enforced; a low share means segmentation is in its early stages.
rpt_rule_b006_why: One host reaching many others on management ports is the typical shape of worm propagation and of pivoting after a compromise.
rpt_rule_b007_why: One account reaching many hosts is a pattern common to automated reconnaissance and credential stuffing; confirm with the account's owner whether the work is expected.
rpt_rule_b008_why: A sudden high-volume transfer is what data being staged or sent out looks like; check it against its purpose to confirm whether the work is expected.
rpt_rule_b009_why: The more connections there are between environments, the more easily a problem in one reaches another.
rpt_rule_l001_why: Telnet and FTP send user names and passwords in cleartext; anyone on the network can read them.
rpt_rule_l002_why: These discovery protocols can be used to impersonate host names and capture account hashes, without any authentication.
rpt_rule_l003_why: A database should be reachable only from its own app; the more apps can reach it, the more likely a single lateral move leads straight to the data.
rpt_rule_l004_why: Once the environment boundary is crossed, someone in a lower-security environment can read Production data directly.
rpt_rule_l005_why: Active Directory is the domain's authentication authority; the more apps can reach it, the greater the chance the domain is enumerated and taken over.
rpt_rule_l006_why: Compromising this host opens every host it can reach over allowed management ports.
rpt_rule_l007_why: An unmanaged host is not controlled by the PCE; when it can reach critical services it is an uncontrolled way in.
rpt_rule_l008_why: No rule allows these paths; until the hosts are enforced, each one is a lateral-movement path that works today.
rpt_rule_l009_why: The report sees only the volume and the destination; whether it is data leaving needs checking against the program on the host and its purpose.
rpt_rule_l010_why: When management ports cross environments, one compromised environment opens the others.

rpt_rdy_sec_how: How this report is worked out
rpt_rdy_how_intro: Each app gets a score from 0 to 100 for one question: if its hosts were enforced now, would normal traffic be blocked? The higher, the safer to enforce. The score adds up the five factors below by their points; a factor without data is left out and the others scaled up.
rpt_rdy_measures_policy: Of the connections into the app with a reported decision, the share an allow rule permits.
rpt_rdy_measures_ringfence: Of the connections into the app, the share that come from the app itself: the fewer outside sources, the easier to ring-fence. Every connection counts, with or without a decision: this measures where connections come from, not what was decided.
rpt_rdy_measures_enforcement: Of the app's managed hosts, the share already enforced (selective counts half).
rpt_rdy_measures_staged: Of the connections with a reported decision, the share not reported as potentially blocked, which enforcement would block.
rpt_rdy_measures_remote: Of the remote-access connections (SSH, RDP, WinRM and the like) with a reported decision, the share a rule permits.
rpt_rdy_full_policy: Every connection in has a rule.
rpt_rdy_full_ringfence: Every connection in comes from the app itself.
rpt_rdy_full_enforcement: Every host is in full enforcement.
rpt_rdy_full_remote: Every remote-access connection has a rule.

rpt_rdy_means_c: Rules still missing: work on the factor that loses the most points first.
rpt_rdy_means_d: Most connections have no rule yet: enforcing now would block a lot of normal traffic.
rpt_rdy_means_f: Not started: most connections have no rule and the hosts are not enforced. Start by writing rules.

rpt_sec_no_previous_parts: The last day of the previous period has no snapshot of ransomware protection, so the two scores rest on different parts and are not compared.
rpt_sec_sec_how: How the maturity score is worked out
rpt_sec_how_intro: One score from 0 to 100 for how far segmentation has come: are hosts enforced, does policy cover the traffic, are management ports and unmanaged sources kept in check. It adds up the five parts below by their points; a part without data is left out and the others scaled up. “This period” shows where the points were lost.
rpt_sec_how_decided: The three parts scored on a share of connections count only the connections with a decision; a connection without one is left out. This is so from 6.10.0: a score in a report made by an earlier version cannot be compared directly.
rpt_sec_measures_enforcement: Of the managed hosts, the share enforced (selective counts half).
rpt_sec_measures_policy: Of the connections with a decision, the share an allow rule permits.
rpt_sec_measures_lateral: Connections on management ports (SSH, RDP, SMB…) with a decision that were not blocked, against the connections with a decision: none scores full, 30% or more scores 0.
rpt_sec_measures_managed: Connections with a decision that come from unmanaged sources (no VEN), against the connections with a decision: none scores full, 50% or more scores 0.
rpt_sec_measures_ransomware: Of the critical and high ransomware-risk services the PCE rated, the share protected.
rpt_sec_full_enforcement: Every host is in full enforcement.
rpt_sec_full_lateral: No management-port connection gets through unblocked.
rpt_sec_full_managed: Every connection comes from a managed host.
rpt_sec_full_ransomware: Every critical and high service is protected.
rpt_sec_means_a: In place: most hosts enforced, most traffic covered by rules. Keep watching.
rpt_sec_means_b: Nearly there: close the part that loses the most points.
rpt_sec_means_c: Under way: clear gaps remain; start with the part that loses the most points.
rpt_sec_means_d: Early: most traffic has no rule or most hosts are not enforced.
rpt_sec_means_f: Not started: almost no rules or enforcement, so lateral movement is unrestricted.
rpt_rw_how_intro: Every number here comes from the PCE's own ransomware ratings: which high-risk services (SMB, RDP, WinRM…) each host listens on and whether policy protects them. The three lists say what to do; the scores show where each host stands.
rpt_rw_tbl_terms: What the numbers and lists mean
rpt_rw_term_pce_means: The PCE's own protection score for the host. The vendor counts only enforced hosts: Full protects every high-risk service, Selective only the ones a Deny Rule blocks, Visibility Only and Idle none (0%). Weighted by severity, 0–100%, higher is better.
rpt_rw_term_pce_use: Compare hosts, lowest first. To raise a host's score: Full, or Selective with Deny Rules on its high-risk services.
rpt_rw_term_computed_means: The same share added up here from each service's protection state, following the vendor's rule for the host's mode. It cannot see which addresses a Deny Rule covers, so it is approximate.
rpt_rw_term_computed_use: Where it differs much from the PCE score, go by the PCE score.
rpt_rw_term_exposure_means: The PCE's ransomware exposure rating for the host (critical, high, medium, low).
rpt_rw_term_exposure_use: Hosts rated critical or high come first.
rpt_rw_term_contradiction_means: The PCE score and the approximation differ by more than 25 points. Usually a Selective host: the PCE counts only what Deny Rules block, which the approximation cannot see.
rpt_rw_term_contradiction_use: Not ranked here; go by the PCE score. The host's explanation says how to raise it.
rpt_rw_term_state_means: Protected: a rule or enforcement stops traffic to the service. Unprotected: any source can reach it. Unknown: the PCE gave no state.
rpt_rw_term_state_use: Unprotected services are the ones in the three lists.
rpt_rw_term_priority_use: Write rules for the sources that use the service, then close it to everyone else.
rpt_rw_term_safe_use: Block it now (a deny rule, or turn the service off): no source seen in 30 days is affected.
rpt_rw_term_suspicious_use: Find out who tries to connect: a scan, or a leftover setting.
rpt_rw_explain_open: {n} high-risk service(s) unprotected ({names}): see this host in “Fix first” and “Safe to block now”.
rpt_rw_explain_contradiction: The PCE scores it {pce}, the services' states add up to about {computed}: as {mode}, the PCE counts only what Deny Rules block, which the states cannot show. Go by the PCE score; to raise it, block its high-risk services with Deny Rules, or move it to Full.
rpt_rw_finding_priority: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) are in use
rpt_rw_finding_priority_why: They are open to any source and were reached in the last 30 days: ransomware can spread through them from those sources.
rpt_rw_finding_priority_action: Follow “Fix first”: write rules for the sources using each service, then close it to everyone else.
rpt_rw_finding_safe: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) can be blocked now
rpt_rw_finding_safe_why: Nobody reached them in the last 30 days, yet any source could.
rpt_rw_finding_safe_action: Follow “Safe to block now”: a deny rule or turning the service off affects no source seen.
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) could not be sorted by use
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted_why: Sorting them into “Fix first” and “Safe to block now” needs the last 30 days of traffic, which this install does not keep (lightweight mode).
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted_action: See each host's unprotected services under “Hosts and their scores”; to have them sorted automatically, switch to alert mode on the Data collection page.
rpt_rw_explain_open_unsorted: {n} high-risk service(s) unprotected ({names}). Whether anyone uses them is unknown (no traffic kept), so they are in no list: decide which must stay reachable, and protect the rest.
rpt_rw_explain_unenforced: The PCE scores it {pce}: the host is {mode}, and the vendor counts only Selective or Full hosts as protected. Full, or Selective with Deny Rules on its high-risk services, makes it count.
gui_reports_desc_policy_usage: Which rules the period's traffic used and which it did not, which Deny Rules blocked something, and which connections no rule allows — counted by the PCE itself. With Rule Hit Count on, also how often each provisioned rule was really hit.
rpt_pu_failed: The PCE could not recompute the period's traffic against the draft policy ({error}).
rpt_pu_unsupported: This PCE does not recompute traffic against the draft policy, so rule usage cannot be counted.
rpt_pu_how_intro: This report answers one question: in the period, which rules did traffic actually use? The PCE recomputes the period's traffic against the Draft policy and names, for each connection, the rule that allows it or the Deny Rule that blocks it. That is not the Rule Hit Count, which counts what the VENs enforced under the Active policy: those counts are the chapter “{chapter}”. With nothing pending, Draft and Active are the same policy.
rpt_pu_how_terms: “Not used” means no traffic in the period matched the rule: it may be no longer needed, or its traffic is rare (month-end, backups). Check each one before removing it, and for rare traffic use a longer period. “No rule allows” means the connection passes now only because the destination is not enforced, or will be blocked once it is.
rpt_pu_pending_intro: Whether the policy this report counted is the one in force.
rpt_pu_pending_none: Nothing is pending: the Draft policy is the same as the active policy, so this report describes the rules in force.
rpt_pu_pending_some: The Draft policy differs from the active policy: {n} change(s) are not provisioned yet. This report counts the Draft; a rule listed below may not be in force yet, or may already be gone from it.
rpt_pu_used_intro: Rules that allowed at least one connection in the period, the busiest first.
rpt_pu_none_used: No rule allowed any connection in the period.
rpt_pu_unused_intro: Enabled rules no connection in the period matched. Candidates to review, not to delete outright: see “How this report is worked out”.
rpt_pu_none_unused: Every enabled rule was used in the period.
rpt_pu_unused_hedge: In the traffic read: {n} window(s) reached the PCE's limit and were cut short, so a rule may have been used in what was not read.
rpt_pu_disabled_intro: Disabled rules never match, so they are listed apart rather than as unused.
rpt_pu_deny_intro: Deny Rules (and Override Deny) that the recompute shows blocking connections in the period.
rpt_pu_none_deny: No Deny Rule blocked a connection in the period.
rpt_pu_no_rule_intro: Connections that no rule allows and no Deny Rule blocks, by source and destination app and service: each needs a rule, or a decision that it should be blocked.
rpt_pu_none_no_rule: Every connection in the period is allowed by a rule or blocked by a Deny Rule.
rpt_pu_finding_unused: {n} rule(s) were not used in the period
rpt_pu_finding_unused_why: A rule nothing uses still opens a path: if it is no longer needed it is attack surface.
rpt_pu_finding_unused_action: Check each rule in “Rules no traffic used” with its owner; for traffic that happens rarely (month-end, backups) run the report over a longer period first.
rpt_pu_finding_pending_why: This report counts the Draft policy, which differs from the policy in force.
rpt_pu_finding_pending_action: Provision or discard the pending changes, or read this report as describing the Draft.
rpt_pu_quality_source: Counted by the PCE: the period's traffic recomputed against the Draft policy, a day at a time; a connection both ends reported counts once.
rpt_pu_quality_truncated: {n} window(s) reached the PCE's per-query limit and were cut short: counts are of the traffic read.
rpt_rw_explain_mismatch: The PCE scores it {pce}, but as a {mode} host it should count every high-risk service as protected (about {computed}): the PCE's numbers disagree; check the host on the PCE console.
rpt_rw_explain_mode_unknown: The PCE scores it {pce}; the host's enforcement mode is not known here, so its services cannot be judged. It shows once the next inventory collection reads it.
rpt_pu_kpi_read_only: In the traffic read: some windows were cut short.
rpt_pu_finding_unused_read: {n} rule(s) were not used in the traffic read
rpt_pu_quality_undetermined: {n} connection(s) got no Draft decision from the PCE: they count neither for a rule nor as “no rule allows”.
pce_write_key_hint: Used only for Rule Hit Count: turning it on from this product and producing its report. The PCE allows both only for the Owner role. Leave blank if you turn Rule Hit Count on in the PCE console; everything else uses the key above.
rhc_reason_not_configured: The PCE connection is not set up yet.
rhc_reason_unreachable: Could not read the Rule Hit Count settings from the PCE.
rhc_reason_unsupported: This PCE has no Rule Hit Count report: it needs PCE 23.5.10 or later (on-premises) or 24.2.0 or later (SaaS).
rhc_reason_needs_write_key: Only the PCE Owner role can read whether the Rule Hit Count report is on. Add a write key with the Owner role under System › PCE connection.
rhc_reason_write_key_denied: The write key cannot read the Rule Hit Count report template: it needs the PCE Owner role.
rhc_reason_partial_template: The VENs record rule hits, but the PCE's Rule Hit Count report is off.
rhc_reason_partial_ven: The PCE's Rule Hit Count report is on, but no VEN records rule hits (firewall settings).
rhc_err_no_write_key: Turning on Rule Hit Count needs a write key with the PCE Owner role. Add one under System › PCE connection.
rhc_err_unsupported: This PCE has no Rule Hit Count report: it needs PCE 23.5.10 or later (on-premises) or 24.2.0 or later (SaaS).
rhc_err_refused: The PCE refused: the write key needs the Owner role.
rhc_err_refused_saas: The PCE refused. On SaaS, Illumio does not allow turning on Rule Hit Count through the API: ask your Illumio account team or open a support case to turn it on.
rhc_err_unreachable: Could not reach the PCE; nothing was changed after the last step listed.
rhc_err_pending_firewall: The firewall settings already have Draft changes that are not provisioned. Provisioning would send those to every VEN too, so nothing was changed. Review them in the PCE (provision or revert), then try again.
rhc_err_step_failed: A step failed; the steps listed before it were done.
rhc_err_pull_refused: The PCE refused to produce the Rule Hit Count report: it needs a key with the Owner role, and the report turned on.
rhc_err_pull_failed: The PCE could not produce the Rule Hit Count report.
rhc_err_pull_timeout: The PCE did not finish the Rule Hit Count report in time.
rhc_err_pull_download: The Rule Hit Count report could not be downloaded from the PCE.
rhc_err_csv_columns: The Rule Hit Count report from the PCE does not have the expected columns (Rule HREF, Rule Hit Count).
rhc_intro: The PCE's own count of how often each provisioned rule was hit; the “{report}” report shows it in its chapter “{chapter}”. It must be on in two places: the PCE's report template, and the VENs (firewall settings). Until both are on, that chapter says why it has no counts; the rest of the report is made as usual.
rhc_saas_note: On SaaS, Illumio does not allow turning this on through the API: the PCE will refuse. Ask your Illumio account team or open a support case to turn it on.
rhc_confirm_intro: This will do the following on the PCE, stopping at the first step that fails:
rhc_confirm_provision: The last step provisions firewall settings to every VEN. Only firewall settings are provisioned; nothing else in Draft is. If firewall settings already have Draft changes, nothing is done.
rhc_step_pce_report_template: Turn on the PCE's Rule Hit Count report template
rhc_step_ven_firewall_settings_draft: Set every VEN to record rule hits (firewall settings, Draft)
rpt_unavailable_rhc_off: Rule Hit Count is not on. Turn it on under System › Report settings.
rpt_unavailable_rhc_unsupported: This PCE has no Rule Hit Count report (it needs PCE 23.5.10 or later on-premises, 24.2.0 or later on SaaS).
rpt_unavailable_rhc_unknown: Cannot tell whether Rule Hit Count is on; see System › Report settings for why.
rpt_err_rhc_merged: Rule Hit Count is now part of the “Policy usage” report; use that report.
rpt_rhc_kpi_hit: Rules in force: hit in the period
rpt_rhc_none_hit: No rule was hit in the period.
rpt_rhc_none_zero: Every recorded rule was hit at least once.
rpt_rhc_none_no_record: Every enabled provisioned rule has a record.
rpt_rhc_sec: Hits on the rules in force
rpt_rhc_intro: How often each provisioned (active) rule was hit in the period, as counted by the VENs and reported by the PCE's own Rule Hit Count report: which of the rules in force are actually used. The other chapters recompute the period's traffic against the Draft; this one is what the VENs enforced under the Active policy.
rpt_rhc_failed: The hit counts and the rules in force could not be read from the PCE ({error}).
rpt_rhc_how_terms: Hit: a connection the rule decided (allowed, or blocked for a Deny Rule). 0 hits: the PCE has a count for the rule and it is 0 for the period. No record: the PCE has no count for the rule — it was provisioned during or after the period, Rule Hit Count was turned on after the period started, or no VEN reported on it. No record is not the same as 0.
rpt_rhc_zero_intro: Provisioned and counted, but nothing hit them in the period. An allow rule at 0 is a candidate for review; one for a rare job (yearly batch, disaster recovery) can legitimately stay at 0. A Deny Rule at 0 only means nothing tried the path it blocks.
rpt_rhc_no_record_intro: Enabled provisioned rules the PCE has no count for. Not evidence that a rule is unused: check when it was provisioned and when Rule Hit Count was turned on. The table “{table}” (when present) lists rules the PCE's report includes with 0 that had no count in the period — only in Draft, deleted since, or created after the period ended: they are not 0.
rpt_rhc_finding_zero: {n} provisioned allow rule(s) had 0 hits in the period
rpt_rhc_finding_zero_why: A rule nothing uses still opens a path an attacker could use.
rpt_rhc_finding_zero_action: Check with the application owners whether each rule is still needed; remove or narrow the ones that are not.
rpt_rhc_quality_source: The hit counts in “{chapter}” come from the PCE's Rule Hit Count report, counted by the VENs; the PCE keeps them 90 days.
rpt_rhc_quality_unparsed: {n} row(s) of the PCE's report had a hit count that could not be read; they are left out, not counted as 0.
rpt_rhc_quality_gone: {n} counted rule(s) are no longer in the provisioned policy (deleted or changed since); they are listed under the ruleset name the PCE reported.
rhc_err_firewall_changed: Draft firewall settings changed while Rule Hit Count was being turned on (someone else edited them), so nothing was provisioned. The VENs' Rule Hit Count setting is in Draft: review firewall settings in the PCE and provision or revert them.
rhc_err_pce_changed: The PCE connection was changed while Rule Hit Count was being turned on; it stopped after the steps listed.
rpt_title_policy_diff: Policy changes waiting to be provisioned
gui_reports_desc_policy_diff: What provisioning the Draft would change: rule sets, rules, IP lists, services and label groups, risky changes first, with who changed them.
rpt_pdf_err_read: Could not read the policy from the PCE, so nothing was compared.
rpt_pdf_none_rules: No rule changed inside a ruleset that exists in both.
rpt_pdf_none_objects: No IP list, service or label group changed.
rpt_pdf_none_other: Nothing else is waiting to be provisioned.
rpt_pdf_how_intro: This report compares the Draft policy with the policy in force (active) at the moment it runs: what provisioning the Draft would add, remove or change. Risky changes come first; each change shows who last changed it, from the PCE events this product has collected.
rpt_pdf_how_terms: Added: only in Draft (created when provisioned). Removed: only in force (deleted when provisioned). Changed: in both, different. High risk: something being disabled (e.g. a Quarantine ruleset: containment goes away), or an IP list, service or label group widened while allow rules in force use it. Medium: re-enabled, or removed. A new ruleset is shown as a whole, with how many rules it brings.
rpt_pdf_summary_same: The Draft is the same as the active policy: provisioning now would change nothing.
rpt_pdf_summary_some: Provisioning the Draft now would make {n} change(s).
rpt_pdf_risk_intro: High first, then medium. Review these before provisioning.
rpt_pdf_rule_sets_intro: Rulesets added, removed, or changed (name, enabled, description, number of rules).
rpt_pdf_rules_intro: Allow rules, Deny Rules and Override Deny inside rulesets that exist in both Draft and active.
rpt_pdf_sec_objects: IP lists, services and label groups
rpt_pdf_objects_intro: Member order does not count as a change. “Lets more through”: the Draft adds members.
rpt_pdf_sec_other: Other items waiting to be provisioned
rpt_pdf_other_intro: Items the PCE lists as waiting that this report does not compare field by field (for example firewall settings or virtual services). Review them in the PCE.
rpt_pdf_finding_disabled_why: Provisioning turns it off everywhere; if it contains or blocks something, that stops.
rpt_pdf_finding_widened_why: Allow rules in force use it: provisioning widens what they allow.
rpt_pdf_finding_action: Confirm the change with whoever made it before provisioning.
rpt_pdf_finding_other: {n} other item(s) are waiting to be provisioned
rpt_pdf_finding_other_why: They go out with the next full provision but are not compared here.
rpt_pdf_finding_other_action: Review them in the PCE before provisioning.
rpt_pdf_quality_live: Draft and active policy read from the PCE at {at}.
rpt_pdf_quality_who: “Last changed by” comes from the PCE events this product collected in the period: who made the newest event on that object; a ruleset also counts the events of its rules. A change outside the period, or before collection started, shows “No event in the period”.
rpt_pdf_quality_who_limited: Only the newest {n} policy events in the period were read for “last changed by”.
rpt_err_format_unsupported: This report type does not make that format.
rpt_mail_files_too_large: The files are too large to attach (over {mb} MB together); download them from the Reports page.
rpt_title_policy_resolver: Policy in force, expanded to IP addresses
gui_reports_desc_policy_resolver: Every rule in force expanded to source IP × destination IP × port, as JSON and CSV for other tools (for example a comparison with traditional firewall rules).
rpt_prs_err_read: Could not read the policy, workloads or policy objects from the PCE, so nothing was expanded.
rpt_prs_finding_omitted: {n} row(s) were left out: the report keeps at most {cap}
rpt_prs_finding_omitted_why: The rulesets cut short ({rulesets}) end with a row saying how many were left out; a tool importing the rows does not get them.
rpt_prs_finding_omitted_action: Narrow the broad rules (e.g. {example}) or compare the rulesets cut short in the PCE.
rpt_prs_finding_capped: {n} rule(s) were too broad to list address by address
rpt_prs_finding_capped_why: Their larger side is a summary like “<5000 hosts: expansion capped>”, marked in the truncated column; it is not an address.
rpt_prs_finding_capped_action: Treat these rows as “many hosts”, not as a list to import.
rpt_prs_quality_live: The policy in force, workloads and policy objects read from the PCE at {at}.
rpt_prs_quality_omitted: {n} row(s) left out at the {cap}-row limit; see the rows marked total_row_cap.
rpt_prs_none: The PCE's active policy holds no ruleset.
rpt_prs_finding_no_address: {n} rules produced no row: no address to expand
rpt_prs_finding_no_address_action: This happens when the labels, label groups or IP lists a rule names resolve to no host address at the moment. Nothing to do if that is expected (for example a quarantine label no host carries now); otherwise check the rule's source, destination and ruleset scope on the PCE.
rpt_prs_side_scope: source and destination are never in the same scope
rpt_prs_how_intro: This report expands every enabled rule in force (allow rules, Deny Rules, Override Deny) into source IP × destination IP × port rows, from the PCE when it runs. The rows are in the JSON and CSV files.
rpt_prs_how_columns: Columns (the same in every language): {columns}. ANY means any address or port (a rule with no source or no service); {ams} is every workload's address, not ANY. A service with no ports (unknown, or process-based) is shown as such, not as any port. Rulesets limit the destinations to their scope; excluded addresses and IP-list exclusion ranges are taken out. Unmanaged workloads with labels are included.
rpt_prs_finding_not_expanded: {n} rule(s) could not be expanded faithfully
rpt_prs_finding_not_expanded_why: They use virtual services (whose services come from the virtual service) or refer to something the PCE does not hold. Each has a row saying so (truncated = not_expanded); none is widened or dropped silently.
rpt_prs_finding_not_expanded_action: Compare these rules in the PCE by hand.
migrate_schedule_unreadable: Not a schedule 5.x could read; skipped.
migrate_schedule_type_unknown: Report type {type} does not exist in v6 (5.x did not run it either); skipped.
migrate_schedule_app_missing: An application summary without an application: 5.x refused to run it; skipped.
migrate_schedule_cron_paused: A cron expression v6 schedules cannot hold: carried as a weekly schedule, paused. Set its time and turn it on.
migrate_schedule_type_paused: A schedule type or weekday 5.x could not run: carried paused. Check its time and turn it on.
migrate_schedule_filter_paused: Traffic filters are not carried (running without them would report more than 5.x did): paused. Add the filter and turn it on.
migrate_schedule_never_ran: 5.x never ran this schedule (a report type or weekday it did not recognize); carried with what it meant, paused. Turn it on if you want it.
wb_search: Host, IP, process or user (part of it)
wb_search_actor: Who did it (part of the name)
wb_dims_hint: The top values under the current conditions. Click one to add it.
wb_empty: Nothing matches these conditions in the period.
wb_gaps: {n} part(s) of the period have no collected data; what is shown leaves them out.
wb_truncated: Part of the period was read only partly (the PCE's answer was capped).
wb_from_pce: Part of this was read from the PCE now (not collected).
wb_limit_hit: More rows match than are shown; narrow the conditions.
wb_bytes_coverage: Only {pct}% of the flows report bytes; a bytes measure reflects that part only.
wb_latency: The newest collected data is {minutes} minutes old.
wb_pull_failed: Could not read the period from the PCE: {error}
wb_pulled: Read from the PCE for this page: {start} – {end}, {rows} rows, at {at}. Kept 30 minutes for the next clicks.
wb_pulled_capped: The read stopped at its row limit; the period after {from} is not included.
wb_pulled_truncated: {n} window(s) of the read were capped by the PCE; some connections in them are missing.
wb_archived: This page is read from the archive, not from the PCE: the period {start} – {end} is older than the kept traffic; archive files of {days} day(s), {first} to {last}, were read: {rows} rows, at {at}. Kept 30 minutes for the next clicks.
wb_archived_missing: The archive has no file for these {n} day(s); their traffic is not on this page: {days}.
wb_archived_unreadable: {n} line(s) of the archive files could not be read and are not counted.
wb_archived_capped: Reading the archive stopped at its row limit; the period after {from} is not included.
wb_pulling: Reading the period from the PCE (about half a minute per day)…
wb_pce_switched: The PCE was changed while this was being read; run it again.
home_focus_not_computed: The focus list is computed every hour and has not been computed yet.
home_focus_stale: Last computed at {time}: more than two hours without an update, so this list may be out of date.
home_focus_empty: Nothing to look at right now.
home_focus_status_missing: not computed yet, its items are missing from the list
home_focus_status_stale: out of date (missed an hourly run)
home_focus_status_error: the last computation failed, its items may be missing
hosts_unmanaged: An address the PCE does not manage: only its traffic is known.
hosts_not_in_inventory: This Workload is no longer in the inventory (deleted, or not yet read): only its traffic and events are shown.
hosts_exposure: Can reach {now} hosts over management ports now; {enforced} once enforced.
hosts_pivot: It is a pivot: paths to critical assets go through it.
hosts_asset_sources: As a critical asset, {n} hosts can reach it now.
hosts_mode_switch: Would be blocked after a switch to Full: by source
hosts_mode_switch_ports: Would be blocked after a switch to Full: by port
hosts_mode_switch_full: This host is already in Full: Potentially Blocked traffic here is from before the switch.
hosts_tamper_none: No tampering in the last 60 days.
hosts_tamper_no_signal: This VEN version does not report which process changed the firewall: the events below carry no process.
hosts_tamper_no_process: This kind of event carries no process information
hosts_tamper_notes_hint: A known cause groups its tampering events: they are counted, not alerted one by one.
hosts_rw_contradiction: The PCE's score and its own service details disagree: the score is not used for ranking.
hosts_rw_none: The PCE lists no high-risk service on this host.
hosts_rw_allow_hint: Sources a rule lets in still count as attack surface: that is the vendor's design.
hosts_rw_allow_button: Find the rules that let sources in (asks the PCE)
home_focus_more: The top {shown} of {total} are shown: show all
hosts_rw_details_stale: The PCE's rating of this host changed after its details were read: the details below are older; the next inventory run reads them again.
hosts_rw_details_missing: The ransomware details of this host have not been read from the PCE yet (or the reads failed): nothing can be said about its services.
hosts_rw_details_not_rated: The PCE gives this host no ransomware protection rating.
home_focus_detections_capped: {total} detections this week; the list was built from the top {considered}.
lat_err_not_computed: Compute the exposure from the PCE first: the simulation runs on that graph.
lat_not_computed: The exposure is computed every hour and has not been computed yet.
lat_collection_off: Traffic is not collected, so there is no exposure to show.
lat_lightweight_intro: Lightweight mode keeps no traffic. Computing reads only the management-port connections of the chosen days from the PCE; the result is kept for 30 minutes.
lat_computing_hint: This can take a few minutes for a large estate or a long period.
lat_computed: Computed {at}, from the connections seen {start} – {end}, up to {hops} hops.
lat_stale: This result is more than 2 hours old: the hourly computation has not run since. Check the background jobs.
lat_period_note: Computed from {days} days pulled for this page, not the {setting}-day observation period set for full mode.
lat_unknown_edges: {n} connections have no reported decision: counted in "now" as not blocked, not counted once enforced.
lat_limit_assets: More than 50 critical assets: the least reachable ones show their numbers only, without paths or cuts.
lat_limit_cross_env: Cross-environment connections are more than shown: the list keeps the first 500 (allowed ones first).
lat_limit_groups: The summary by {key} keeps the 2,000 largest group pairs.
lat_limit_other: Part of the result was cut at a limit.
lat_now_hint: Allowed and Potentially Blocked connections: not enforced, so they get through.
lat_enforced_hint: Only the connections an allow rule covers.
lat_pivots_hint: Hosts whose removal would split the graph: the way between otherwise separate parts.
lat_pivot_gone: no longer a pivot once enforced
lat_critical_not_set: No critical assets are set, so paths and cut points cannot be shown. The reach ranking below covers every host.
lat_assets_none: No critical asset appears in the inventory.
lat_asset_sources: {now} hosts reach {asset} within {hops} hops now; {enforced} once all enforced.
lat_asset_unreachable: No host reaches this asset over management ports.
lat_asset_numbers_only: Beyond the 50 most reachable assets: numbers only.
lat_cuts_none: No single cut lowers the reach.
lat_cut_edge: Cut only {src} → {dst} on {ports}: hosts reaching {asset} go from {before} to {after}.
lat_cut_node: Deny everything into {host}: hosts reaching {asset} go from {before} to {after}.
lat_reach_hint: How many hosts each host reaches over management ports within {hops} hops.
lat_host_not_in_graph: {host} has no management-port connection in this period.
lat_groups_hint: Each cell counts host pairs with a management-port connection; red: some are Allowed (they stay once enforced), amber: Potentially Blocked at most.
lat_groups_later: The summary by Label comes with the next computation.
lat_footholds_hint: Hosts whose high-risk services the PCE rates unprotected and listening (ransomware protection).
lat_init_coverage: Management-port flow records in the last {days} day(s): {total}; {user} ({user_pct}) name the initiating user and {process} ({process_pct}) the initiating process. The rankings below cover only the records that carry the field.
lat_init_none_users: No management-port flow record names a user.
lat_init_none_processes: No management-port flow record names a process.
lat_init_none_system: No system account on management-port flow records.
lat_init_need_mode: These rankings need kept traffic: switch to alert or full mode.
lat_init_collection_off: Traffic is not collected, so there is nothing to rank.
lat_init_capped: The ranking read its first {n}; more exist and are not counted.
lat_init_capped_system: Only the first {n} accounts were checked; the accounts after them were not.
lat_init_none_system_capped: No system account among the first {n} accounts; the accounts after them were not checked.
rpt_lat_init_capped: The ranking read its first {n}; more exist and are not counted.
rpt_lat_init_capped_system: Only the first {n} accounts were checked; the accounts after them were not.
rpt_lat_init_none_system_capped: No system account among the first {n} accounts; the accounts after them were not checked.
lat_detections_need_mode: Detections need the traffic of every collection cycle: switch to alert or full mode.
lat_detections_none: No detection in the last 7 days.
lat_detections_more: Showing the {shown} most important of {total} detections in the last 7 days.
lat_rule_node: Deny everything into {host} (on the way to {asset})
lat_sim_readonly: Read-only: computed from the observed traffic; nothing is written to the PCE.
lat_sim_node_inbound: The rule blocks only connections into the host; its own connections out are untouched, so it still counts as a source.
lat_sim_limit_hit: The lists below are cut at their limit.

guide_ev_tampering: The VEN found its firewall changed outside the PCE and restores the policy itself; what matters is who changed it. Check the process and PID above (when given); unless another firewall program or an administrator's manual change explains it, treat the host as possibly compromised.
guide_ev_suspend: A suspended VEN removes every firewall rule on the host and lets all traffic through: the host is unprotected. Confirm someone suspended it to troubleshoot; if not, treat it as an attack, and unsuspend it as soon as possible.
guide_ev_clone: One VEN identity is on a cloned host. In the PCE's VEN list, filter on "VEN clone detected"; where it is not remediated automatically, deactivate and unpair the cloned VEN, then pair it again.
guide_ev_missed_heartbeats: The PCE has not heard from these VENs for a quarter of the offline timer (15 minutes by default). Check whether the hosts are down or cannot reach the PCE; at the offline timer (60 minutes by default) the PCE removes them from other hosts' rules.
guide_ev_offline: The PCE marked them offline and took their addresses out of other hosts' rules, so other hosts can no longer reach them. If a host is still running, restore its connection to the PCE; a planned shutdown can be ignored.
guide_ev_lost_agent: The PCE deleted this host, but its VEN is still running and no longer managed. Confirm the deletion was intended; pair the VEN again to keep the host protected.
guide_ev_login_failed: Repeated failed sign-ins to the PCE. In the PCE console's events, look at the source address and account: if it is not someone you know, block the source and check the account did not sign in afterwards.
guide_ev_api_authn: The PCE refused API credentials: usually a key that expired, was deleted or is mistyped. Look at the event's source: for an automation, renew its credentials; for this illumio-ops, check the key in System › PCE connection; an unknown source is someone guessing credentials.
guide_ev_api_authz: A valid API key lacks the permission for this action. Check whether the caller's role should have it; for this illumio-ops, check the keys' roles in System › PCE connection (rule scheduling, quarantine and RHC use the write key).
guide_ev_policy_apply: The VEN could not apply the latest policy and keeps the previous one. Usual causes: a faulty custom iptables rule, or a policy that would cut the VEN off from the PCE. On the host, check every VEN process runs (illumio-ven-ctl status) and look for errors in the VEN logs.
guide_ev_policy_change: Rule sets or rules were changed. Confirm the change was expected; what is not provisioned yet can be reviewed item by item in the report Policy changes waiting to be provisioned, and takes effect only when provisioned.
guide_ev_provision: A policy version was provisioned and is in force. In the PCE's policy versions, see what changed and who provisioned it; an unexpected change can be reverted to the previous version on the PCE.
guide_ev_api_key: An API key calls the PCE with its owner's permissions for as long as it exists. For a new key, confirm who made it and why; a deleted key that an automation (this illumio-ops included) still uses makes it fail.
guide_ev_unpair: These hosts' VENs were removed and the PCE no longer manages them; their firewall is whatever was chosen at unpairing: remote management only, the rules from before the VEN, or all open. Confirm this was a planned retirement; if not, pair them again soon.
guide_ev_auth_settings: The PCE's sign-in settings changed (local password policy or SAML, for example). Confirm who changed them and that it was expected; an unexpected change may be someone keeping a way in.
guide_sys_pce_health: While the PCE health check fails, events and traffic may not come in. See which step fails in System › PCE connection; for an on-premises PCE, check its services on the PCE host.
guide_sys_collection_failing: No data is coming in, so detections and reports miss this period. Act on the error (key, network, PCE timeout); once it recovers, check the gaps in System › Modes and data sources and backfill where needed.
guide_sys_data_loss: Data is missing for this period: what happened then is not detected and not in reports. See the gaps in System › Modes and data sources; a period the PCE still keeps can be backfilled.
guide_sys_job_failing: This background job keeps failing, and what it does has stopped. See which in System › Background jobs, and the error in System › Logs.
guide_sys_disk_low: When the disk is full, data cannot be written. Shorten the retention in System › Modes and data sources or the report retention in System › Report settings, or add disk space.
guide_sys_siem_backlog: The SIEM destination is taking events more slowly than they come, or cannot be reached. See its state and last error on the SIEM forwarding page; events that could not be sent can be reviewed and resent from the DLQ.
guide_high_blocked: Many connections were blocked by policy. On the Investigate page, see who was blocked and where they were going: normal business needs a rule; a scan or probing points at the source host.
guide_det_fanout: Check whether this host is an admin jump host or a scanner. If not, see on the Investigate page which program made the connections and to which hosts; quarantine it if needed. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_new_admin_connection: Check this new admin connection matches known work (maintenance, a deployment). If not, look at the program and account on the source host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_pivot_chain: The middle host is being used as a stepping stone. Investigate it first: who signed in and what ran; quarantine it if needed to cut the path. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_blocked_surge: This host tried many blocked destinations, typical of scanning or malware probing. See its blocked connections and programs on the Investigate page, then investigate the host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_non_admin_group: A host outside the admin group used an admin port. If it should, add it to the admin group (System › Lateral movement settings); if not, find out who is using it. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_cross_env: An admin connection crosses environments, letting a weaker one reach a stronger one. Confirm it is needed; if not, block it with a rule. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_account_fanout: One account reached many hosts in a short time. Check what the account is for (service, administrator); if unusual, disable or reset it and check the hosts it reached. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_unexpected_initiator: This program does not normally start this kind of connection. In the host profile, check where the program comes from and who runs it. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_peer_deviation: None of its group did this before. Check for a new deployment or configuration change; if there is none, investigate the host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_volume_surge: The host's traffic is far above its 7-day high. See on the Investigate page which destination and program carry it: known work (backups, updates) can be ignored; otherwise check whether data is leaving. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_account_new_source: The account signed in from this host for the first time. Confirm with its user (a new machine or place); if not, reset the account's password and investigate the source host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_suspicious_tool: Attackers often use this program to move inside a network. Confirm it is an administrator's known work; if not, find who ran it and consider quarantining the host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_new_process: This program made connections from this host for the first time. Check whether it is newly installed or updated software. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_auth_to_non_dc: Authentication or directory traffic went to a host that is not a directory server: a rogue service or a misconfiguration. Check the destination's role; if it is a directory server, list it in System › Lateral movement settings. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_new_dc_client: This host contacted the directory server for the first time. A host that just joined the domain is normal; an existing host that starts querying the directory may be gathering account information. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_directory_surge: Directory queries surged, typical of account enumeration or password spraying. Find the program and account making them on this host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_direction_reversal: Connections between these hosts always went the other way. Check for an architecture or configuration change; if there is none, investigate the initiating host. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_new_pair_port: These hosts started using a new port: the destination may be running a new service. Check the program behind that port on the destination is expected. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_quiet_host_wakes: A long-quiet host became active. Confirm someone brought it back into use; idle hosts are a common place to hide. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_data_staging: Several internal hosts sent data to this host, a common step before exfiltration. Check it is known work (backups, reporting); if not, see where the host sends the data next. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
guide_det_off_hours: The host was active at an hour it usually is not. Check for a scheduled job or someone on duty. If it is normal, mark it known below and the same pattern stops alerting.
rpt_err_before_archive: The period starts before any data that can be read: neither the store nor the archive has older traffic. Start it on or after the earliest day the date field allows.
rpt_err_period_not_over: Reports count whole days: the last day can be yesterday at the latest.
rpt_quality_archive_flows: Traffic from {first} to {last} ({n} days) comes from the archive: the store no longer keeps those days.
rpt_quality_archive_events: Events from {first} to {last} ({n} days) come from the archive: the store no longer keeps those days.
rpt_quality_archive_missing: {n} days are in neither the store nor the archive, and the report leaves them out: {days}.
rpt_quality_archive_unreadable: {n} archive records could not be read (a damaged file or an unknown format) and are not in the report.
rpt_quality_archive_truncated: Loading from the archive stopped at {n} records: archived data after {start} is not in the report. Shorten the period.
gui_reports_period_hint: Whole days in the display time zone, both ends included; from {first} to {last}. Days the store no longer keeps are read from the archive, and the report says so.
err_siem_tls_unverified: Certificate verification is off for {names}: the lines are encrypted, but anyone who can answer in the SIEM's place receives them. Save only if you accept that.
siem_tls_unverified_warning: Certificate verification is off: the connection is encrypted, but whether it reaches your SIEM is not checked.
siem_rate_1h: Last hour: {rate}% went through ({sent} of {tried} attempts)
siem_rate_1h_none: Last hour: nothing sent or tried
siem_sends_hint: Sent: lines the destination took. Failed: once for each run the destination could not be reached, and once for each line it refused or that could not be formatted. Counted in 10-minute steps, so each period can reach up to 10 minutes further back.
siem_dlq_full_hint: Held at a record the full DLQ has no room for: nothing after it is sent. Resend or purge DLQ lines and it goes on by itself.
siem_dlq_retention_hint: Lines moved to the DLQ longer ago than this are deleted once a day. 0 keeps them until they are resent or purged.
siem_dlq_none_match: No DLQ line has an error containing that text.
siem_dlq_confirm_purge_older: Purge every line moved to the DLQ more than {days} days ago (of the destination chosen above)? They cannot be brought back.
siem_dlq_full_line: The whole line as it was formatted for the destination ({n} characters); a resend sends exactly this.
fleet_inventory_never: The inventory has not been read from the PCE yet: every count is zero until it is.
fleet_online_rule: Online: the PCE marks the VEN online and its last heartbeat is within an hour; lost contact counts from the last heartbeat (the VEN status report's definitions).
fleet_none_hosts: No managed host in the inventory.
fleet_list_limit: Showing the first {shown} of {n}: narrow the filter to see the rest.
fleet_none: No managed host matches the filter.
fleet_unnamed: Workload …{id} (the PCE sent no host name)
fleet_enf_intro: Moves the chosen hosts forward to the target mode with the write key, after this preview and your confirmation. Forward only: Idle → Visibility Only → Selective → Full; moving back is done in the PCE. Hosts not chosen are never changed.
fleet_enf_labels_hint: The managed hosts carrying every Label below (at most {max}).
fleet_enf_no_match: No managed host carries every one of these Labels.
fleet_no_write_key: No write key is set: nothing can be changed. Set the optional write key on the PCE connection page.
fleet_reason_unmanaged: Not a managed host: not changed.
fleet_reason_not_in_inventory: Not in the inventory: not changed.
fleet_reason_same_mode: Already in this mode: not changed.
fleet_reason_not_forward: Not forward from its mode: change it in the PCE.
fleet_reason_mode_changed: Its mode changed after the preview: not changed.
fleet_blocks_title: What Full would block: connections into each host, last 7 days
fleet_blocks_rule: Counted: connections into the host reported Potentially Blocked, which no rule in the active policy allows and Full blocks. Connections its VEN did not report are not counted.
fleet_blocks_selective: Selective blocks only the connections a Deny Rule names; the reported decisions do not say which rule, so no count is given. Check the Deny Rules in the PCE before moving.
fleet_blocks_none: Visibility Only blocks nothing: the VEN reports traffic and applies no rule.
fleet_truncated: A count stopped at its row limit: the numbers are at least what is shown.
fleet_enf_confirm: I have checked the hosts and what would be blocked, and move {n} hosts to {mode}.
fleet_enf_heartbeat: The PCE accepted the change; each VEN applies it at its next heartbeat, and the PCE shows the policy syncing until then.
fleet_status_unknown: No answer: check it in the PCE
fleet_detail_pce_changed: The PCE connection changed during the batch: not written.
fleet_rate_intro: The PCE has each chosen host's VEN report traffic more often for {minutes} minutes (how often is the PCE's choice), then every 10 minutes again by itself (the PCE console's Increase Traffic Update Rate). With the write key; nothing else changes.
fleet_rate_offline: Some chosen hosts are not online: their VENs report nothing until they are back.
fleet_rate_until: Until {at}; after that the VENs report every 10 minutes again.
fleet_rate_again: To keep it longer, ask again after it ends.
fleet_history_none: Nothing has been changed from this page yet.
fleet_err_no_write_key: No write key is set: nothing was changed.
fleet_err_pce: The PCE could not be read or written: {error}
fleet_err_too_many: {n} hosts carry these Labels; at most {max} at a time. Add a Label to narrow it.
pce_events_timeout_hint: How long one /events request may take, 5–600 seconds. Blank: {seconds} seconds for this deployment type (SaaS answers /events slowly).
migrate_fleet_progressions_not_in_v6: the VEN enforcement progression records of 5.x are not carried into the v6 fleet action history. The file stays in the 5.x directory.
err_backfill_traffic_not_collected: Lightweight mode does not collect traffic, so traffic cannot be backfilled. Switch to alert or full mode first, or backfill events only.
backfill_sources_hint: Lightweight mode collects no traffic, so it backfills events only. Traffic goes back as far as flows are kept, events as far as events are kept.
retention_run_intro: Retention clean-up runs once a day and deletes data older than the retention days above (with archiving on, only days already archived). Run it now after shortening a retention period.
retention_run_queued: Retention clean-up started. Its result shows under Background jobs as Retention clean-up.
err_pce_target_needs_choice: The address changed and data has been collected from {old}. Choose below whether {new} is the same PCE.
pce_choice_intro: Data has been collected from {old}. Is {new} the same PCE at a new address?
pce_choice_keep: Same PCE: keep the collected data
pce_choice_clear: Another PCE: clear the collected data
pce_choice_hint: Keeping is checked first: a few stored workloads are read from the new address with the API key above, and only if that PCE answers for them is anything saved; the data, alert history, rule schedules and reports then belong to the new address. Clearing removes the collected traffic, events and analysis; settings, alert history and reports stay, and archive files are moved aside.
pce_kept_notice: Saved as the same PCE at a new address: the collected data, alert history, rule schedules and reports now belong to it.
err_pce_not_the_same: The PCE at the new address knows none of the {n} stored workloads checked, so it is not the same PCE. Nothing was saved. Check the address, or choose “Another PCE” to clear the data.
err_pce_same_nothing_to_compare: No workload of this organization has been collected yet, so the new address cannot be checked against stored data. Nothing was saved. Choose “Another PCE” instead.
err_pce_same_unverifiable: The new address could not be checked ({reason}). Nothing was saved. Check the address, the TLS setting and the API key, then try again.
err_pce_keep_needs_same_org: Data can be kept only for the same organization; the organization ID changed, so this is another PCE.
rs_check_paused: A paused schedule is not checked; resume it first.
rs_check_switched: {name}: checked now; the target was switched and provisioned.
rs_check_none: {name}: checked now; the target is already as planned, nothing was changed.
rs_check_skipped: {name}: checked now and skipped: the target or its rule set has a change not yet provisioned, it is not provisioned, or the PCE no longer has it.
rs_check_failed: {name}: checked now and failed; the PCE's answer is in the latest run below.
rs_err_paused: That schedule is paused; resume it before checking it.
rs_err_rulesets_read: The rule sets could not be read from the PCE: {error}
rsb_count_limited: The PCE returned {total} rule sets; the first {n} are shown. Search by name to narrow them.
rsb_none: The PCE has no active rule set with that name.
rsb_no_rules: This rule set has no rules.
err_invalid_username: The username must be 1 to {max} characters (spaces at either end are removed).
security_username_hint: Changing the username takes the current password. Like a password change, everyone else who is signed in is signed out; this browser stays signed in under the new name.
security_username_changed: Username changed. Everyone else who was signed in has been signed out.
collection_clear_intro: Clearing removes everything collected from the PCE: traffic, events, workloads, the baseline and the analysis results. Settings, alert records, rule schedules and generated reports stay; archive files are moved aside, not deleted. Collection and a first backfill then start again.
collection_cleared: The collected data was cleared; collection and a first backfill start again.
err_clear_confirm_mismatch: Type {word} to confirm; nothing was cleared.
err_clear_store_busy: The data could not be cleared now: a long read was still using it. Nothing was deleted; try again in a minute.
rpt_ven_online_intro: Every online VEN with its version, operating system, mode, last heartbeat, policy sync and compatibility. The compatibility count below covers every managed host, online or not.
rpt_ven_none_online: No VEN is online: none is marked online by the PCE with a heartbeat in the last hour.
rpt_ven_quality_compat: Compatibility comes from the PCE's compatibility report for each VEN (green: pass; yellow: warning; red: fail), read once a day for hosts in Idle (the PCE writes it while a VEN is in Idle); next to a warning or fail are the checks the PCE did not pass. {n} hosts have no report or have not been read yet and are unknown.
rpt_ven_quality_compat_oldest: The oldest compatibility report the PCE holds for these hosts was written {at}.
rpt_ven_find_offline_why: A VEN that is not reporting gets no policy updates and sends no traffic.
rpt_ven_find_offline_action: Go through the table of VENs not reporting: confirm whether each host is shut down or retired; for one still running, check the VEN service and its connection to the PCE.
rpt_ven_find_tamper_why: Tampering with no known cause means something other than the PCE is changing these hosts' firewalls and nobody has recorded what it is.
rpt_ven_find_tamper_action: Open the host page of each host in the tampering table with an unexplained count above 0: annotate a known cause, or find out who changed the host firewall.
rpt_ven_find_sync_title: {n} online VENs without their policy in place
rpt_ven_find_sync_why: These hosts are online but are not running the PCE's current policy.
rpt_ven_find_sync_action: Work through the problems listed for each host in the policy sync table.
rpt_ven_find_compat_title: {n} Idle hosts did not pass the compatibility check
rpt_ven_find_compat_why: The PCE found something on these hosts that gets in the way of the VEN enforcing policy.
rpt_ven_find_compat_action: Before moving a host out of Idle, deal with the checks listed in the compatibility column of the online VENs table.
rpt_inv_tbl_conflicts: Endpoints seen with more than one label combination
rpt_inv_conflicts_none: Every managed endpoint in the period's flows carried one label combination.
rpt_inv_conflicts_note: An endpoint above carried different labels on different flows in the period: it was relabelled during the period, or the two ends of a connection reported different labels. Rules written against labels treat each combination differently; check the host's current labels in the PCE. At most 5 combinations are listed per endpoint.
rpt_aud_sec_failed_change: Failed sign-ins followed by a high-risk change
rpt_aud_failed_change_intro: A high-risk change ({changes}) by a user, preceded within {minutes} minutes by a failed sign-in or denied request ({failures}) under the same user name or from the same source address. A real PCE records a failed sign-in without a user name, so the address is usually what matches; an address shared by several people (a jump host, NAT) matches them all. One row per change.
rpt_aud_none_failed_change: No high-risk change came within {minutes} minutes after a failed sign-in by the same user name or from the same source address.
rpt_aud_failed_change_title: {n} high-risk changes right after failed sign-ins
rpt_aud_failed_change_why: A guessed or stolen password looks like this.
rpt_aud_failed_change_action: Confirm with each user that they made the change; if not, revert it, reset the credential and review the account's other actions.
rpt_new_disappeared_intro: Connections (source, destination, port and protocol) seen in the previous period of the same length and not seen since this period began. Connections on dynamic ports ({port} and up) or without a port are left out, as for new connections. The previous period here is the one the other metrics compare with.
rpt_new_tbl_disappeared: Seen in the previous period, not since
rpt_new_disappeared_none: Every connection seen in the previous period was seen again in this one.
rpt_new_disappeared_unknown: Which connections stopped cannot be said: the previous period was not collected in full, or is older than the connection baseline keeps.
rpt_trf_rate_note: {rated} of {total} flow records with byte counts were seen for at least a second, so they have a rate: their bytes over the time from first to last detection. The PCE reports no transfer duration, so this rate is a lower bound of the real one (highest here: {max} Mbps).
rpt_trf_rate_none: None of the {total} flow records with byte counts was seen for a second or more, so no rate can be given.
rpt_trf_no_rate: No flow record with byte counts was seen for a second or more.
rpt_trf_tbl_per_conn: Most bytes per connection (records of more than one connection)
rpt_trf_no_multi_conn: No flow record with byte counts holds more than one connection.

cond_transmissions_hint: None ticked: any transmission. A connection the PCE reported without one is never left out.
